questions.question: Why is Layer 2 considered an attractive target for attackers in modern networks?
questions.option_a: A. Layer 2 protocols were designed with strong built-in authentication and encryption.
questions.option_b: B. Layer 2 protocols such as Ethernet, ARP, DHCP and VLAN trunking were largely designed for trusted, physically-controlled networks and have little to no built-in authentication.
questions.option_c: C. Compromising Layer 2 has no effect on higher-layer security controls.
questions.option_d: D. Layer 2 traffic is always encrypted end-to-end by default.
questions.explanation: Layer 2 protocols were built assuming a trusted physical environment, so a compromise at this layer can undermine security controls operating above it.

questions.question: What is the primary security benefit of segmenting a network into VLANs?
questions.option_a: A. It increases the size of the broadcast domain.
questions.option_b: B. Devices on different VLANs cannot reach each other without going through a router, limiting the impact of a compromise in one segment.
questions.option_c: C. It eliminates the need for any Layer 3 security controls.
questions.option_d: D. It automatically encrypts all inter-VLAN traffic.
questions.explanation: VLANs create separate logical broadcast domains, so a compromise in one VLAN does not automatically expose devices in other VLANs.

questions.question: What is the native VLAN and why is leaving it as the default (VLAN 1) considered a security risk?
questions.option_a: A. The native VLAN carries all tagged traffic; leaving it as VLAN 1 improves compatibility.
questions.option_b: B. Frames on the native VLAN are sent untagged across a trunk; using the default VLAN 1 makes double-tagging attacks easier because many access ports also default to VLAN 1.
questions.option_c: C. The native VLAN is never used on modern switches.
questions.option_d: D. Changing the native VLAN has no security impact.
questions.explanation: The untagged nature of the native VLAN is exactly what the double-tagging attack abuses; keeping it on VLAN 1 aligns it with the default access VLAN.

questions.question: Which protocol automatically negotiates whether a link becomes a trunk and is therefore exploitable for switch spoofing?
questions.option_b: B. VTP
questions.option_c: C. DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol)
questions.option_d: D. STP
questions.explanation: DTP automatically negotiates trunk mode with no authentication, allowing an attacker to force a port into trunk mode.

questions.question: How does a CAM-table (MAC-flooding) attack work?
questions.option_a: A. The attacker changes its own MAC address to match a legitimate device.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker floods the switch with frames carrying different fabricated source MAC addresses until the CAM table fills and the switch begins flooding frames out all ports.
questions.option_c: C. The attacker sends double-tagged frames to reach another VLAN.
questions.option_d: D. The attacker runs a rogue DHCP server.
questions.explanation: Switches have finite CAM tables and are designed to fail open (flood like a hub) when the table is full, allowing the attacker to receive traffic not intended for them.

questions.question: Why does a switch’s ‘fail-open’ design make a CAM-table attack possible?
questions.option_a: A. When the CAM table is full the switch drops all traffic for security.
questions.option_b: B. When the CAM table is full the switch prioritises availability and floods unknown-destination frames out every port, turning itself into a hub.
questions.option_c: C. The switch always verifies the legitimacy of every source MAC before learning it.
questions.option_d: D. Fail-open mode encrypts all flooded frames.
questions.explanation: The design choice prioritises continued forwarding over confidentiality, which an attacker exploits by filling the table.

questions.question: What is the main difference between MAC-address spoofing and a CAM-table attack?
questions.option_a: A. Both attacks fill the CAM table with fake addresses.
questions.option_b: B. MAC spoofing changes the attacker’s own MAC to impersonate a specific device; a CAM-table attack floods many different MACs to overflow the table.
questions.option_c: C. MAC spoofing only works on wireless networks.
questions.option_d: D. There is no practical difference.
questions.explanation: MAC spoofing is identity theft of one address; CAM flooding is a denial-of-service / eavesdropping attack that overwhelms the switch’s learning table.

questions.question: Why is relying solely on MAC-based port security (sticky MAC) insufficient against MAC-address spoofing?
questions.option_a: A. Sticky MAC permanently locks every possible MAC address.
questions.option_b: B. An attacker can wait until the legitimate device disconnects or spoof during an idle window and still present the authorised MAC.
questions.option_c: C. Port security automatically uses 802.1X.
questions.option_d: D. Sticky MAC prevents any MAC from ever changing.
questions.explanation: MAC addresses are software-configurable; once the legitimate device is offline the attacker can simply claim its MAC.

questions.question: What is the strongest mitigation against MAC-address spoofing?
questions.option_a: A. Increasing the CAM-table size.
questions.option_b: B. 802.1X / centralised AAA authentication that ties access to a verified credential rather than a MAC address.
questions.option_c: C. Disabling all access ports.
questions.option_d: D. Using only static ARP entries.
questions.explanation: 802.1X authenticates the user or device identity, so simply cloning a MAC is no longer sufficient to gain network access.

questions.question: How does switch-spoofing (VLAN hopping) work?
questions.option_a: A. The attacker sends double-tagged frames on an access port.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker’s device mimics a switch speaking DTP; if the connected port has DTP enabled it becomes a trunk and the attacker receives traffic for all VLANs on that trunk.
questions.option_c: C. The attacker floods DHCP Discover messages.
questions.option_d: D. The attacker poisons ARP caches.
questions.explanation: DTP has no authentication, so an attacker can negotiate a trunk and gain visibility into every VLAN carried on that trunk.

questions.question: Why is the command ‘switchport nonegotiate’ an effective, low-cost fix for switch spoofing?
questions.option_a: A. It encrypts all trunk traffic.
questions.option_b: B. It disables DTP so the port can never auto-negotiate into a trunk, removing the attack surface with a single configuration line.
questions.option_c: C. It changes the native VLAN.
questions.option_d: D. It enables Dynamic ARP Inspection.
questions.explanation: Disabling DTP completely prevents the automatic trunk negotiation that switch spoofing relies on.

questions.question: Describe the VLAN double-tagging attack.
questions.option_a: A. The attacker forces a port into trunk mode with DTP.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker on the native VLAN crafts a frame with two 802.1Q tags; the first switch strips the outer (native) tag and the next switch delivers the frame into the target VLAN identified by the inner tag.
questions.option_c: C. The attacker floods the CAM table.
questions.option_d: D. The attacker runs a rogue DHCP server.
questions.explanation: The attack abuses the fact that native-VLAN frames travel untagged; only the outer tag is stripped, leaving the inner tag for the next switch.

questions.question: Why does the double-tagging attack only work in one direction (attacker to target VLAN)?
questions.option_a: A. Because return traffic is always encrypted.
questions.option_b: B. There is no symmetric path back through the same untagged native-VLAN mechanism for the reply frames.
questions.option_c: C. Because switches drop all return traffic by default.
questions.option_d: D. Because the attacker’s port is automatically shut down.
questions.explanation: The attack relies on the one-way stripping of the outer tag; replies do not automatically reverse the same path.

questions.question: Why does moving the native VLAN off VLAN 1 mitigate double-tagging?
questions.option_a: A. It encrypts native-VLAN traffic.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker’s access port is no longer on the native VLAN by default, so the outer tag no longer matches and the attack fails.
questions.option_c: C. It disables 802.1Q entirely.
questions.option_d: D. It forces all ports into trunk mode.
questions.explanation: When the native VLAN is an unused VLAN that no access ports belong to, the attacker cannot place the required outer tag.

questions.question: What does a DHCP-starvation attack achieve for the attacker?
questions.option_a: A. It allows the attacker to intercept traffic by becoming the default gateway.
questions.option_b: B. It exhausts the legitimate DHCP server’s IP address pool so new legitimate clients cannot obtain an address (Denial of Service).
questions.option_c: C. It forces all ports into trunk mode.
questions.option_d: D. It poisons ARP caches.
questions.explanation: By sending Discover messages with many different spoofed MACs the attacker consumes every available lease.

questions.question: How does DHCP spoofing differ from DHCP starvation?
questions.option_a: A. They are identical attacks.
questions.option_b: B. Starvation exhausts the address pool (DoS); spoofing runs a rogue DHCP server that answers first and sets the attacker as gateway/DNS, creating a MITM position.
questions.option_c: C. Spoofing only works on wireless networks.
questions.option_d: D. Starvation requires a trunk port.
questions.explanation: Starvation is a resource-exhaustion attack; spoofing is an impersonation attack that redirects traffic.

questions.question: How does DHCP Snooping mitigate both DHCP starvation and DHCP spoofing?
questions.option_a: A. It encrypts all DHCP messages.
questions.option_b: B. It classifies ports as trusted or untrusted; server responses are accepted only from trusted ports, and rate-limiting on untrusted ports blunts starvation floods. It also builds a binding table used later by DAI.
questions.option_c: C. It disables DHCP entirely.
questions.option_d: D. It forces every client to use static IP addresses.
questions.explanation: Trusted/untrusted port distinction stops rogue servers, while rate-limiting and the binding table address starvation and enable further controls.

questions.question: Why must Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) be configured after DHCP Snooping?
questions.option_a: A. DAI has nothing to do with DHCP Snooping.
questions.option_b: B. DAI validates ARP packets against the IP-to-MAC binding table that DHCP Snooping builds; without that table DAI has no trusted data source and cannot function correctly.
questions.option_c: C. DHCP Snooping requires DAI to be enabled first.
questions.option_d: D. The order does not matter.
questions.explanation: DHCP Snooping populates the binding table that DAI uses to decide whether an ARP claim is legitimate.

questions.question: What would happen if you enabled Dynamic ARP Inspection without DHCP Snooping already running?
questions.option_a: A. DAI would automatically create its own binding table.
questions.option_b: B. DAI would have no valid binding information and would either drop legitimate ARP traffic or be unable to distinguish forged replies, effectively breaking ARP or providing no protection.
questions.option_c: C. All ports would automatically become trusted.
questions.option_d: D. The switch would fall back to static ARP only.
questions.explanation: Without the binding table produced by DHCP Snooping, DAI lacks the reference data needed to validate ARP packets.

questions.question: How does ARP spoofing establish a man-in-the-middle position?
questions.option_a: A. By flooding the CAM table.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker sends forged (gratuitous) ARP replies telling each victim that the other victim’s IP is at the attacker’s MAC, so both victims send traffic through the attacker.
questions.option_c: C. By negotiating a trunk with DTP.
questions.option_d: D. By exhausting the DHCP pool.
questions.explanation: Hosts accept unsolicited ARP replies and update their caches, allowing the attacker to redirect traffic in both directions.

questions.question: What is the root cause that makes ARP spoofing possible?
questions.option_a: A. ARP packets are always encrypted.
questions.option_b: B. Hosts accept unsolicited ARP replies and update their ARP cache without verifying that a request was ever sent.
questions.option_c: C. Switches never learn MAC addresses.
questions.option_d: D. ARP uses TCP instead of UDP.
questions.explanation: The lack of any authentication or request-response binding in ARP is the fundamental vulnerability.

questions.question: A network administrator must choose between leaving port security disabled or enabling it with a maximum of 2 MAC addresses and violation mode ‘restrict’ on every access port. What is the operational cost of the second option and is it worth it?
questions.option_a: A. Zero operational cost and it is always worth it.
questions.option_b: B. Slightly higher configuration and monitoring effort (tracking legitimate MACs, handling false positives) but the security gain against CAM flooding and basic MAC spoofing is substantial and generally worth the cost.
questions.option_c: C. Extremely high cost that outweighs any benefit.
questions.option_d: D. It completely eliminates the need for any other Layer-2 controls.
questions.explanation: Port security adds modest operational overhead but closes a major attack vector with a simple, low-cost control.

questions.question: Which two outcomes can a CAM-table attack produce depending on attacker intent?
questions.option_a: A. Only eavesdropping.
questions.option_b: B. Quiet eavesdropping (when the table is full traffic is flooded to the attacker) or performance-degrading Denial of Service (sustained flooding).
questions.option_c: C. Only Denial of Service.
questions.option_d: D. Only VLAN hopping.
questions.explanation: The same technique can be used for passive interception or for degrading switch performance, depending on how long the flood continues.

questions.question: Which two plausible outcomes can DHCP spoofing produce?
questions.option_a: A. Only Denial of Service.
questions.option_b: B. Man-in-the-middle interception (by setting the attacker as gateway/DNS) or Denial of Service (if the rogue server gives invalid configuration).
questions.option_c: C. Only trunk negotiation.
questions.option_d: D. Only MAC-table overflow.
questions.explanation: A well-configured rogue server yields MITM; a broken one simply cuts victims off.

questions.question: A small company has no Layer-2 security controls configured. Which three mitigations would you prioritise first, considering both risk and ease of implementation?
questions.option_a: A. 802.1X everywhere, static ARP on all hosts, and VTP pruning.
questions.option_b: B. Port security on access ports, disable DTP (switchport nonegotiate), and move the native VLAN off VLAN 1.
questions.option_c: C. Only Dynamic ARP Inspection, only DHCP Snooping, and only 802.1X.
questions.option_d: D. Increase CAM-table size, enable VTP, and leave native VLAN as 1.
questions.explanation: These three are high-impact, low-to-medium configuration cost controls that immediately close the most common and easily exploited attack vectors.

questions.question: What does the DHCP Snooping binding table contain and why is it important?
questions.option_a: A. Only MAC addresses of trusted ports.
questions.option_b: B. Mappings of MAC ↔ IP ↔ VLAN ↔ port learned from legitimate DHCP transactions; it becomes the trusted data source for Dynamic ARP Inspection.
questions.option_c: C. Only the IP addresses of rogue servers.
questions.option_d: D. Encryption keys for ARP packets.
questions.explanation: The binding table is the foundation that allows DAI to validate ARP claims.

questions.question: In the context of port-security violation actions, what is the functional difference between ‘shutdown’ and ‘restrict’?
questions.option_a: A. Both actions are identical.
questions.option_b: B. Shutdown disables the port entirely (preventive); restrict drops violating traffic but keeps the port up and generates a log/alert (detective).
questions.option_c: C. Restrict disables the port; shutdown only logs.
questions.option_d: D. Neither action has any security effect.
questions.explanation: A single keyword change moves the same feature from a purely preventive control to a detective control.

questions.question: Why is physical security an effective complementary control for many Layer-2 attacks?
questions.option_a: A. It has no relationship to Layer-2 security.
questions.option_b: B. If an attacker cannot physically reach a switch port or cable, CAM flooding, MAC spoofing, rogue DHCP and ARP spoofing are all simultaneously prevented without any configuration.
questions.option_c: C. Physical security only protects against Layer-3 attacks.
questions.option_d: D. Physical locks automatically enable 802.1X.
questions.explanation: Many Layer-2 attacks require the attacker to be on the local wire; physical access control removes that opportunity.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct layered-defense baseline for Layer 2?
questions.option_a: A. Only port security on trunk ports.
questions.option_b: B. Port security on every access port, DTP disabled everywhere, native VLAN moved off VLAN 1, DHCP Snooping enabled, and Dynamic ARP Inspection layered on top.
questions.option_c: C. Only static ARP entries and increased CAM-table size.
questions.option_d: D. Leaving all defaults and relying on Layer-3 ACLs.
questions.explanation: No single control covers every attack; the listed combination forms a practical, layered baseline.

questions.question: An attacker sits on an access port that belongs to the native VLAN and sends a double-tagged frame. What happens on a correctly hardened switch where the native VLAN has been moved to an unused VLAN?
questions.option_a: A. The frame is delivered into the target VLAN.
questions.option_b: B. The attack fails because the outer tag no longer matches the native VLAN, so the frame is not treated as untagged native traffic.
questions.option_c: C. The switch automatically converts the port to a trunk.
questions.option_d: D. The frame is flooded to all VLANs.
questions.explanation: Moving the native VLAN away from any access-port VLAN breaks the outer-tag match required by the attack.

questions.question: Which mitigation technique simultaneously helps against both CAM-table attacks and basic MAC-address spoofing?
questions.option_a: A. Disabling DTP only.
questions.option_b: B. Port security with a low maximum MAC count and sticky learning plus a violation action.
questions.option_c: C. Changing the native VLAN only.
questions.option_d: D. Enabling VTP pruning.
questions.explanation: Limiting the number of learned MACs stops flooding; sticky learning plus violation handling makes simple spoofing harder.

questions.question: Why can the same Layer-2 attack technique be aimed at different goals?
questions.option_a: A. Because every attack has only one possible outcome.
questions.option_b: B. Attacker intent, not a difference in the technique itself, determines whether the result is eavesdropping, DoS, access, or enabling a further attack.
questions.option_c: C. Because switches randomly choose the outcome.
questions.option_d: D. Because all attacks always produce DoS.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises that every attack maps to at least two outcome categories; the technique stays the same while the goal changes.

questions.question: What is the main security implication of the fact that Layer-2 protocols have little or no built-in authentication?
questions.option_a: A. Higher-layer controls are automatically protected.
questions.option_b: B. A successful Layer-2 attack can become a foothold for traffic interception, credential theft or pivoting to Layer 3, undermining controls that never get a chance to inspect the traffic.
questions.option_c: C. Authentication is unnecessary at Layer 2.
questions.option_d: D. All Layer-2 traffic is inherently trustworthy.
questions.explanation: Because the ground-floor protocols trust by default, a compromise there can bypass or defeat higher-layer security.

questions.question: In a DHCP Snooping deployment, which ports should be configured as trusted?
questions.option_a: A. All access ports where end users connect.
questions.option_b: B. Uplink ports that lead toward the legitimate DHCP server.
questions.option_c: C. Every port on the switch.
questions.option_d: D. Only ports that belong to VLAN 1.
questions.explanation: Only ports that face the real DHCP server (or other trusted infrastructure) should be trusted so that rogue servers on access ports are blocked.

questions.question: An administrator enables port security with sticky MAC and violation mode shutdown on all access ports. What operational risk remains?
questions.option_a: A. No operational risk remains.
questions.option_b: B. A legitimate device that is replaced or whose NIC is changed will cause the port to shut down until an administrator clears the sticky entry, creating a potential availability issue.
questions.option_c: C. The switch will automatically learn unlimited MACs.
questions.option_d: D. DTP will still negotiate trunks.
questions.explanation: Sticky MAC permanently binds the first learned address; hardware changes require manual intervention.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between DHCP Snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection?
questions.option_a: A. They are completely independent controls.
questions.option_b: B. DHCP Snooping builds the binding table that DAI uses; together they form a clean example of layered defence where one control supplies the trusted data for another.
questions.option_c: C. DAI must be enabled before DHCP Snooping.
questions.option_d: D. Enabling either one automatically enables the other.
questions.explanation: The dependency is intentional and illustrates layered defence within a single switch.

questions.question: A company relies only on MAC-based port security (sticky MAC, no other authentication). Evaluate why this alone is insufficient against determined MAC-address spoofing and recommend a stronger alternative.
questions.option_a: A. It is already sufficient; no further action is needed.
questions.option_b: B. An attacker can still spoof the authorised MAC when the legitimate device is offline; the stronger alternative is 802.1X / centralised AAA that authenticates a credential rather than a MAC address.
questions.option_c: C. Sticky MAC automatically implements 802.1X.
questions.option_d: D. The only solution is to disable all access ports.
questions.explanation: MAC addresses are not strong identities; 802.1X moves the trust decision to a verified credential.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs an attack with a simple configuration mitigation?
questions.option_a: A. Switch spoofing → increase CAM-table size.
questions.option_b: B. Double tagging → switchport nonegotiate.
questions.option_c: C. Switch spoofing → switchport nonegotiate; Double tagging → change native VLAN off VLAN 1.
questions.option_d: D. ARP spoofing → disable DTP.
questions.explanation: Each attack has a distinct, low-cost configuration fix that directly removes its enabling condition.

questions.question: What is the primary reason Layer-2 attacks are often cheap to execute?
questions.option_a: A. They require expensive specialised hardware.
questions.option_b: B. Many need nothing more than a laptop on an access port and freely available tools; the protocols themselves provide no authentication barrier.
questions.option_c: C. They can only be performed by highly skilled nation-state actors.
questions.option_d: D. They always require physical access to the core router.
questions.explanation: The absence of authentication and the abundance of simple tools make these attacks accessible.

questions.question: When evaluating a Layer-2 mitigation, what does LO2 specifically require a student to consider?
questions.option_a: A. Only whether the mitigation has a cool-sounding name.
questions.option_b: B. Whether the mitigation actually closes the gap for all plausible outcomes of the attack, and at what cost/complexity (financial, configuration, computational).
questions.option_c: C. Only the financial cost.
questions.option_d: D. Whether the mitigation is mentioned in the summary slide.
questions.explanation: LO2 is about evaluating trade-offs, not merely naming controls; a mitigation’s value depends on the full range of outcomes it prevents and the real-world cost of deploying it.

questions.question: Which attack is fundamentally a one-way injection attack that cannot easily receive return traffic via the same path?
questions.option_a: A. CAM-table flooding.
questions.option_b: B. ARP spoofing.
questions.option_c: C. VLAN double-tagging.
questions.option_d: D. DHCP starvation.
questions.explanation: Double-tagging relies on the one-directional stripping of the outer native-VLAN tag; there is no symmetric return path.

questions.question: An organisation has implemented port security, disabled DTP and moved the native VLAN. Which additional controls are still required to protect against DHCP and ARP attacks?
questions.option_a: A. Nothing further is required.
questions.option_b: B. DHCP Snooping (with trusted/untrusted ports and rate-limiting) and Dynamic ARP Inspection that uses the resulting binding table.
questions.option_c: C. Only increasing the size of the CAM table.
questions.option_d: D. Only enabling VTP.
questions.explanation: Port security and trunk/native-VLAN hardening do not address the lack of authentication in DHCP and ARP; DHCP Snooping + DAI close those remaining gaps.
